MOTION TO REFER CERTAIN MATTERS TO STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with unanimous consent I move:
That the standing committee on marine and fisheries be authorized to examine and consider (1) the recommendations of the international north Pacific fisheries commission that the stock of halibut in the eastern Bering sea and the stock of herring off the west coast of the Queen Charlotte islands each be exempted from the abstention principle contained in the international convention for the high seas fisheries of the north Pacific ocean, (2) the international convention for the high seas fisheries of the north Pacific ocean, and (3) the last annual report of the international north Pacific fisheries commission and, in particular, to examine and consider the possible harmful effects which such recommendations may have upon Canada's fisheries and with authority to report its findings and recommendations from time to time.
This motion is seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Mather).

speechtext: Has the Canadian government considered the communication from the representatives of the Italian committee in Toronto protesting the C.B.C. camera program depicting the life of Canadians of Italian descent in Toronto and, if so, what action has the government taken with regard to this protest?

maintopic: C.B.C. PROGRAM ON ITALIANS IN TORONTO
speechtext: I am advised by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that the program "Camera Canada" on January 14 was based on the activities of a recently arrived Italian family in Toronto. It was generally well received but was criticized by some members of Toronto's Italian community who would have preferred an emphasis on different features of community life. The C.B.C. arranged for a review of the film by several representatives of the Italian community and discussed their criticisms with them. After a full review of all the circumstances, the C.B.C. still believes that the program was a fair and honest portrayal of the life of a group of recent immigrants from Italy and of their efforts to adapt to life in their new home land.

speechtext:
It is my intention, Mr. Chairman, to make a comprehensive statement on the work of the Department of Labour in introducing the 1962-63 estimates of the department. I hope members of this committee will give every consideration and co-operation as we address ourselves to the various items which are before us in these estimates. I am prepared to reciprocate in like manner and give every co-operation in answering questions which may be in the minds of members. As a result I hope these estimates will be passed expeditiously.
The Department of Labour, during the period in which I have been Minister of Labour, has endeavoured to co-operate with each member of this house in every possible way, and to be as helpful as possible to each and every member of parliament. I doubt very much whether any member, regardless of where he sits in this chamber, has found our attitude to be one of discourtesy or lack of co-operation in giving out information or assisting with regard to any problem which relates to one or another aspect of our work. We have tried to afford this co-operation to all members of parliament for their benefit and for the benefit of their constituents.
I hope in my statement to be able to deal with every aspect of the department and every phase of its jurisdiction. However, to give a complete picture of all the various phases of the department's work and responsibilities would necessarily take up a great deal of the time of this committee. I do not intend to do that, but I shall endeavour to give a brief resume of all the aspects of our work in as few words as possible. After that I hope I shall be in a position to answer any questions which may be in the minds of the members when we reach the particular items in our estimates to which they relate.
Mr. Chairman, the committee will be asked to provide $217,577,700 in the main estimates and $80 million in supplementary estimates (A). The Department of Labour requires

$192,809,700 out of this amount and the unemployment insurance commission requires $104,768,000. This represents an increase of $47,534,597 over the 1961-62 main and supplementary estimates. Members of this committee will notice that this increase in relation to the 1961-62 appropriation does not agree with the figures shown on page 169 of the blue book. The explanation is that further supplementary estimates for 1961-62 totalling about $93,400,000 were passed by the house after the main estimates were prepared and, of course, the $80 million supplementary estimates for 1962-63 are not shown in the summary. The supplementary estimates for 1962-63 to which I have referred include $30 million for the municipal winter works incentive program and an additional $50 million for technical and vocational training organizations.
I should like now to deal generally with the main activities of the Department of Labour. I wish to put on record my sincere appreciation, first of all, of the excellent work performed by the staff of the department and of the co-operation I have received from labour and management groups, the provinces and the many other organizations with which we work across Canada. The high level of competence associated with the work of the department will, I am sure, be a source of satisfaction to all members of this committee, as it is to me.
Vote No. 1 includes costs relating to the general administration of the department, international affairs and the women's bureau. In the field of international affairs, as hon. members know, the department serves as our official link with the international labour organization, and it is this co-ordinating activity which is provided for in the item. The highly constructive work which the I.L.O. carries forward is so well known as not to require recounting at this time. The department has played an increasing role in these significant activities as the I.L.O. becomes increasingly more important in making a special contribution to the manpower and labour relations development of many countries less developed than our own.
In the women's bureau we are interested, of course, in the activities of women in the labour force of this country. Women are playing an increasingly important part in Canada's labour force, and the work of the women's bureau makes a significant contribution to a wider understanding of the problems and needs of women at work in addition to encouraging progressive standards in that field. The bureau works closely with the provincial departments of education and labour, employers' organizations, the labour movement and the national women's organizations.

In the economics and research branch, research plays a key role in the Department of Labour in helping us deal with the complex problems we face in providing a sound factual basis for the development of our programs and policies. The work is carried out by the economics and research branch provided for in vote No. 5. This research has made a vital contribution to the development of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act which was passed by this house in December, 1960, and to the preparation of the industrial change and manpower adjustment act which is now on the order paper to be placed before the house this session. I hope we shall have an opportunity of discussing this legislation.
The results of this research have contributed to our understanding of the consequences of automation to workers, management and governments in Canada, and have made a most practical contribution to the consideration of measures dealing with this important problem. Work on a study of changing technology and manpower in one of the regions of a Canadian railway was completed this year, and a report will be published. Work began on a similar study in two large railway shops and a report on this is under preparation. A second study of the extent of electronic data processing in Canada is under way and a detailed examination of the effects of office automation on manpower and training needs is being carried out. Five reports on studies in other industries have already been issued. A survey of employers' current and future needs for engineers and scientists was conducted during the year and a preliminary report has been issued. The joint federal-provincial studies of seasonal unemployment in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick will be concluded shortly. A range of special studies of the characteristics of the unemployed were initiated during the past year in co-operation with the dominion bureau of statistics. As a result of this, additional information on unemployment has already been published and more information is currently being developed.
In the field of conciliation, during the fiscal year ending March 1962 the more important collective agreements between the major railways and the running trades expired and new agreements were being negotiated. I am pleased to report, Mr. Chairman, that all of these disputes have been settled, including those involving the major railways and the brotherhood of railroad trainmen, the brotherhood of locomotive firemen end enginemen and the brotherhood of locomotive engineers.
Supply-Labour
Collective agreements are to run through to 1964. Also negotiations commenced in the year ending March 31 for the renewal of collective agreements between the major railways companies and the unions representing over 100,000 non-operating employees. A conciliation board was appointed and I am happy to report that in August, for the first time in recent years, a settlement of all issues in dispute was made by the board. I want here to say what tremendous work the hon. member for York South did on the board, representing, as he did, the unions, as one of the members of three.
The field of labour-management co-operation is very important indeed and is a field that has now been recognized by a great many people of this country, in which these same people are beginning to become more interested. As hon. members know, I have stressed the importance for over four and a half years now of developing effective labour-management co-operation in this country in order to improve the performance of our economy and to eliminate the distrust between the parties to industry. I am happy to say that great strides have been made in this respect. The lessons to be learned about the contribution of labour-management co-operation to a more efficient economy and rising standards of living have been emphasized for us by the European experience. The recent national productivity council mission to Europe has emphasized the fundamental need in this country for a substantial development of labour-management-government co-operation. As hon. members know, the productivity council reports both to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and to the Minister of Labour. The council has held two significant labour-management conferences at Kingston and at Halifax which have played an important role in the development of consultation between top level labour and management in this country. In the past year, the Department of Labour has organized area conferences of labour and management at Winnipeg, Cornwall and Kitchener to promote labour-management co-operation through exchange of experience on improving the effectiveness of joint committees. The productivity council as recently as last week held another conference in Saskatoon, and the reports I have received indicate that it was highly successful, in fact more successful probably than some of the others. In other words, we are getting into an area of understanding, where these conferences are beginning to bring about a better understanding of labour and management in their own particular spheres. It is planned to hold more of these conferences over the coming months.

Supply-Labour
All of these conferences have played a significant role in improving the atmosphere of labour-management relations and stimulating discussion of ways and means of bringing about greater labour-management-government co-operation. The labour-management co-operation service of the department is responsible for promoting better labour-management relations throughout Canada. This kind of co-operation at the plant level is one of the important keys to increased productive efficiency and high morale in industry. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that we formed 1,700 such committees at the plant level across this country. We have increased these committees in the past year by 100, and they are doing a very important job in labour-management relations.
I want to remind hon. members that in the field of civilian rehabilitation this house, in May 1961, passed the Vocational Rehabilitation of Disabled Persons Act. That is an important milestone in giving greater economic and social independence to our disabled citizens. Most of the provinces have responded to this legislation by developing a more comprehensive program of vocational rehabilitation. As a result, we have doubled our estimate for this fiscal year, which is only the beginning of a greatly expanded program. Similar substantial increases have been requested in the estimates for vocational training for disabled persons as part of this program. While this government will continue to provide for those unable to provide for themselves, we now know that through the co-operation of provincial governments and voluntary organizations a considerable number of these seriously disabled persons can be usefully employed and can make a contribution to our society.
In the field of special services we have under vote 30 a provision for the special services branch which administers the municipal winter works incentive program, the federal-provincial farm labour program and the program of organized movement of workers between Canada and the United States. It is also involved in our regular winter employment campaign, more familiarly known as the "DO IT NOW" program. I would pay tribute to public-spirited citizens across Canada, the press, radio and television for their co-operation in making this program successful.
Under the farm labour program, agricultural workers are moved within and between the provinces and Canada and the United States to meet seasonal requirements. On October 17 and 18, the department held a most successful conference on training in agriculture. The conference was attended by representatives of provincial departments of education and agriculture, representatives of farm organizations and of industries related to agricul-

ture and of professional agriculturalists. The conference identified and discussed the issues which must be faced in the development of effective agricultural training in Canada and should stimulate the development of greatly improved training programs for agriculture by the provinces under the auspices of the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act.
For a few moments I should like to deal with the municipal works incentive program. Last winter's municipal winter works incentive program gained an increased response from the provinces and municipalities and made a fundamental contribution in securing winter work for thousands of Canadians who would otherwise be unemployed. The 8,269 projects that were authorized provided an estimated 148,000 jobs involving almost 6 million man-days of work. The Canadian Labour Congress in its research bulletin for May and June of 1962 has commended this program in the following words:
There can be no question that the program has been effective and increasingly so-145,000 jobs in the 1961-62 season, lasting an average of about 40 days each for a total of 5,784,374 man-days work -this is not to be sneezed at. Moreover, there is little doubt that at least an equal number of jobs were provided indirectly in the industries which manufacture, sell and transport materials used in these jobs. The program certainly has not solved the problem of seasonal unemployment but it has made a substantial contribution.
In July the government announced that the program would again be in operation this winter on the same basis as last year. All of the provinces accepted this offer and the program got under way on October 15 last. As of January 25 of this year 5,853 projects from 2,293 municipalities have been accepted and approved. The total cost of the projects so far authorized is estimated at something like $319 million. That is, indeed, a substantial public works program for this winter instigated under this program. These projects will provide 107,011 jobs and some 4,949,229 man days of work.
Based on municipal estimates of cost the federal contribution towards these authorized projects is something in the neighbourhood of $35,811,000. These figures represent an increase over last year at the same stage of the program. Since the inception of this program in the fall of 1958 the amount of work provided under the program has increased each and every year and the figures I have quoted with regard to employment provided apply only to on-site employment. It is estimated, as the Canadian Labour Congress points out, that at least an equal number of workers will be employed through the production and supply of materials used on various projects.

I should like to deal for a short while with technical and vocational training in Canada. The provision for the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act is made in votes 35 and 40. The Prime Minister recently described this program as "the most massive effort in the field of human training ever undertaken in Canada".
The program of capital facilities and expanded training programs which the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act provided represents a massive intervention on the part of this government to equip the manpower resources of Canada, and particularly its youth, to meet the economic and technological challenges of the future.
Effective technical and vocational education is a fundamental prerequisite for the development of sound economic growth in Canada. A few of the reasons for this major initiative on the part of this government may be pointed up by some fundamental facts.
Skilled, professional and white-collar occupations make up 70 per cent of our labour force today while the unskilled and semiskilled account for the balance of 30 per cent. Over the past ten years alone, professional workers have grown by 70 per cent; skilled by about 38 per cent and white collar workers by 34 per cent. On the other hand, unskilled and semi-skilled workers have increased by only 19 per cent and some unskilled primary industry occupations have declined in numbers.
This vast upgrading of the educational and training requirements of our labour force has been necessary because this country faced a serious problem of youth leaving school without sufficient educational qualification. About 35 per cent of our young people who entered elementary school in recent years have left school at or before grade 8; another 35 per cent left before obtaining their junior matriculation.
Over the next four years, it is estimated that there will be an increase of 280,000 in the numbers of youth attending secondary schools. Already this program is having a substantial impact on our early-school-leaver problem.
In September there were 80,000 more in the 14-19 year age group than last year, but only
8,000	more youth were in the labour market. This has meant that in spite of the very substantial increase in the numbers of youth in
Supply-Labour
this age group, many more of them are staying in school longer to complete their educational and vocational training.
The capital building program, of which I shall give the members of this committee some detail, at its present stage of development will provide facilities to train almost
130,000	Canadians each and every year. In the light of the figures and the increased number of youth who will be attending school and entering post secondary school training facilities, there is absolutely no reason to fear that these facilities will be underutilized as some critics assert. If anything, they may be overcrowded.
Under this act, between April 1, 1961, when it came into effective operation and January 28, 1963, of this year, I as Minister of Labour have approved for federal contribution 468 provincial capital projects for institutes of technology, adult vocational schools, trade schools, and technical and vocational high schools.
The progress of this technical education and capital building and equipment program is so important and of such interest to every member of this committee, I am sure, that I would request the permission of this committee to table a statistical statement which will indicate the details of this program as of January 28, 1963, by provinces and for Canada as a whole. If I may have this permission at this time, I should be glad.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. As there are many new members of the house who perhaps are not familiar with the contribution which this government has made under this act I should like at this moment to cite its main provisions. Under the act agreements with the federal government were entered into by all the provinces in this country. They provide for a federal contribution of 75 per cent of provincial expenditures on buildings and equipment for vocational training purposes up to March 31, 1963. After March 31, 1963 the federal contribution reverts to the 50 per cent level. In other words, we gave an incentive of an additional 25 per cent up until that time and then the contribution goes back and provides for the paying of 50 per cent from then on.
It is, I think, of special significance that of these 468 projects 226 were for completely new schools. Of the remaining projects 168 were for additions and alterations to or equipment for existing schools or institutes, and 74 were for minor alterations or equipment costing less than $10,000. The total cost of these 468 projects is around $458.1 million and the federal share will be approximately $292.8 million. These figures do not represent the total building program because new building submissions are still being received and new buildings are being forecast by the provinces for the next four years. My original objective in this program will be surpassed by a considerable margin by March of this year.
Training facilities will be available for our Canadian youth and adult workers to enable them to undertake the training they require to follow satisfying careers in skilled and technical occupations and to meet the continually growing needs of our economy. We have other training programs under our jurisdiction and I will deal with them a little later.
The provision of buildings and equipment, of course, only provides the physical facilities for the technical and vocational training. Teachers, courses and the many other aspects of training must be made available and the legislation fully provided for this. There are 10 programs which are being developed under the agreements on a joint federal-provincial basis. They meet almost every conceivable need for training, including the training of technical and vocational teachers.
Supply-Labour
I will mention some of the highlights of some of the more important programs. The federal government contributes 50 per cent of the cost of these federal-provincial programs with the exception of training for the unemployed to which our contribution is 75 per cent. To meet the growing demand for technicians we are providing for post-high school technical programs in all provinces except Prince Edward Island. This is a new and very important area of our manpower development program and will add greatly to the opportunities for our young people and to the total skilled manpower resources of Canada.
The trade and occupational training programs are being expanded and improved in order to provide a wider range of opportunities in the semi-skilled and skilled trades, the service trades and commercial and business occupations. These are, in the main, the pre-employment programs at the trade level.
In the field of upgrading and retraining I would point out that in the past we have not had an extensive program for employed workers through which they can upgrade their knowledge and their skills. New programs are now being developed in co-operation with industry to meet this need of our adult workers. With rapid changes in production and manufacturing techniques, which give rise to new occupations and displacement in others, it is extremely important to provide adequate training services for those who are now employed. In this connection I would mention the project at Leaside, Ontario, where three companies have joined in a training program for their employees in co-operation with the federal and provincial governments. This is a pilot project in this respect. I can foresee great developments in this program which will help to minimize the less desirable effects of technological change in conjunction with the manpower legislation currently before parliament.
For several years we have been developing and expanding our training program for the unemployed. In this area we are contributing 75 per cent of provincial expenditures on this program provided, of course, the province reaches an agreed upon minimum volume of training. In this area there has been an increase which is not entirely to my satisfaction but during the past year the figures that I have available to me show that some 19,000 people have been retrained under this program, and I hope that the provinces will undertake more and more of this work because of the results that have been achieved in those municipalities where the program has been taken seriously. This program is being expanded in all provinces as a significant step

Supply-Labour
in creating much wider employment opportunities for those unemployed who take advantage of it.
I wish I could take the time of the committee to tell members what has been done in this field in the city of Cornwall, Ontario where, upon completion of the St. Lawrence seaway and the closing down of the textile mill, the authorities found themselves at odds as to what to do with the labour force. During the past few years, with everyone working in co-operation with the federal and provincial governments, it has been possible to retrain 800 unemployed workers in that area and place them in useful employment to the extent of some 85 per cent of those who were unemployed before. This is a good example.
In the field of the physically handicapped, the training of physically handicapped persons has been going on for some years and, like our other programs, it too is growing. As new facilities become available we will be able to offer even more to those who are in need of vocational rehabilitation because of some physical handicap.
One of the very important new programs in our agreements is for the training of vocational teachers, supervisors and administrators. Many new and improved programs are developing. The staff of our training institutions and our vocational co-ordinators and supervisors are so important that we must place special emphasis on this program. A lack of adequate programs in Canada in past years resulted in a great shortage of competent people for this work. However, progress already made in planning and establishing facilities and classes provides ample evidence that most anticipated requirements for teaching personnel will be fully met as they arise.
Our apprenticeship program is operating through a ten year agreement with all of the provinces except the province of Quebec. This program provides for the long range development of journeymen in the highly skilled trades, and many changes are taking place in apprenticeship programs to meet current and future needs.
Now for a few moments I should like to deal with employment conditions in Canada. During the past two years, and particularly since the beginning of 1961, production, employment and incomes in Canada have risen substantially. The improvement has been reflected in such economic indicators as the gross national product which in volume terms has increased by 8.8 per cent, and the industrial production index which has risen by 7.9 per cent. Employment in the third quarter of this year was between 4 and 5 per cent higher than two years ago, and 6 per cent higher in non-farm industries.

In addition to the increase in numbers employed, short work weeks have been eliminated in some plants during the past year and substantial overtime has been worked in others. As a result the average work week in manufacturing in the first seven months of this year was almost half an hour longer than the comparable period of 1961, which is a clear sign of the rising level of industrial activity.
Incomes of Canadians have kept pace with the higher levels of average hours and employment. Personal income in the first half of 1962 was 7 per cent higher than the first half of 1961. For those who like to compare incomes in terms of real dollars per capita, let me repeat what I said during the throne speech debate. In the second quarter of 1962 the gross national product per capita, in 1957 dollars and seasonally adjusted at annual rates, was $1,978. This is $65 higher than in 1957, five years ago.
It has been encouraging to note that a good part of the employment expansion of the past year has been in industries that employ a high proportion of male workers, who form a major part of the unemployed. This year manufacturing provided more than
60.000	new jobs, on average. This summer, for instance, construction employment was at its highest level in three years, up 7 per cent over 1961, and the service industries provided 121,000 additional jobs over the past year.
Seasonal factors remain the major influence in creating unemployment in this country. It is worth noting as an example that some six weeks of severe winter in Britain were recently blamed for an increase of some
100.000	in the ranks of the unemployed in that country. This is a problem with which we have to cope in an even more extreme fashion each and every winter.
In December unemployment reached a total of 6.3 per cent of the labour force, compared to 6.4 per cent a year earlier and 8.2 per cent in 1960. More than three quarters of the total number of unemployed had been out of work for less than three months, and the decline in the number of long term unemployed is particularly encouraging. In September less than one fifth of the total had been seeking work for six months or more.
The combination of increasing job opportunities and declining unemployment resulted in scarcities of workers this summer in specific occupations and specific areas despite the fact that the over-all supply of labour was still plentiful. National employment services across the country have reported a substantial

increase in job opportunities this year, and for many jobs qualified applicants were not available.
As most hon. members are aware, the accelerated depreciation program was initiated last year to encourage new firms to locate in areas of heavy unemployment, and to produce new products in Canada generally. The response on the part of municipalities and business interests has been encouraging. In the early part of November accelerated depreciation had been certified for assets valued at a total of $186 million. That is to say $186 million worth of productive facilities had been or are in the process of being installed to produce products that are either new in Canada or are new to a particular area or locality, and these companies will provide some 5,642 new jobs.
These are among the indications of the many forces at work in the economy to sustain and increase the level of activity. Investment has been substantially higher than last year and there is no sign of weakening in this field. Manufacturing has improved in many fields on account of actions taken by the government in recent years and in recent months. A stimulating effect will be provided by the near record western grain crop.
Export and import industries have been aided by dollar devaluation, as it was expected they would be. Domestic demand is expected to remain high because of the increase in consumer savings. The increase in employment last summer was more than normal and it is expected that the drop during the winter months will be below average. In spite of general improvement unemployment remains a serious problem.
As hon. members know, over the past several years a number of measures designed to implement economic expansion have been approved by parliament, and the effect of these measures has been felt in the general upward movement in the economy. These measures have taken the form of increased works projects, incentives to industry and a general upgrading of the labour force through training and retraining. As the full effect of these measures is felt through the economy, the upward movement will continue. An indication of this is to be found in the economic growth figure expressed in the large and continuing increase in gross national product over the past year, in the improved balance of payments situation, in generally improved conditions in industry and in the greatly increased volume of exports.

Mr. Chairman, we have listened with interest to the minister, as we always do. I wish to assure the minister, who is seeking the co-operation of this side of the house to expedite the passing of his estimates, that we are always pleased to co-operate with the genial Minister of Labour. He may be assured that while we shall leave no stone unturned to examine carefully the estimates he has presented, we will afford him the fullest co-operation. It is unquestionable that the minister has a fine department. He has officials who are doing and have done over the past years a very fine job of administration. There is certainly no question about that. We had experience with them in former administrations and I am sure their high calibre has continued into this one.
The minister has painted a picture of very great economic activity and social well being in the country, to which I am afraid we will have to take some exception. I have made a few notes and I should like to refer to some of the remarks made by him. First I wish to say that we have no quarrel with his retraining and training program except, of course, that it has not reached its acme, by any stretch of the imagination, and can be improved upon. But this, in my opinion, is one of the greater accomplishments of the present Minister of Labour. The winter works program was outlined by the minister. The figures in relation to the operation of the winter works program and the co-operation of various municipalities show that the federal government expended some $36 million in the last fiscal year. This required the greatest co-operation on the part of the municipalities with whom the minister was dealing. I think it is certainly a reflection of the very great interest shown by the municipalities which has contributed to the success of this so-called winter works program.
This program, of course, has been made even more urgent since 1957 because unemployment has been such a serious problem since that time. When the figures presented by the minister are considered, together with the assistance which has been given under the unemployment assistance act and the contributions of the municipalities, it adds up to quite a large, glorified relief program. The sum of $319 million was contributed by the

Supply-Labour
municipalities in order to alleviate this serious unemployment situation. On the other hand, in 1961-62 the federal government, under the unemployment assistance act, expended some $92 million, representing part of the relief given to those who were not in a category which would provide them with unemployment insurance. This means that we have expended $184 million in relief measures. We have no figures, of course, to show the amount which must have been expended by the provinces and the municipalities for direct relief. When totalled up it will be seen that our relief programs over the year amounted to many, many millions of dollars. So that while the picture the minister paints in this chamber may have the aspect of an aurora, it is not quite in accordance with the facts.
I should like to go back a short way into the history of this question. Let us see what the government was saying in the early months of last summer in regard to our unemployment situation. I am happy that the minister, at least, before resuming his seat did say that unemployment represented a very serious problem in Canada. On June 13, 1962 the Prime Minister said, "We have the unemployment problem in Canada licked now as a result of the policies we have instituted". I repeat, Mr. Chairman, that the Prime Minister said we had the problem of unemployment licked. How does that square with the facts given to the committee by the minister this afternoon?

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROGRESS TOWARD SOLUTION
speechtext: It is a question of interpretation.

subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO PROGRESS TOWARD SOLUTION
speechtext:
Yes, we do not have the simultaneous interpretation that was requested here this afternoon. The Prime Minister has made quite a number of statements. In all fairness I wish to say that I cannot connect the Minister of Labour with any of these profound statements of untruths that were made during the election campaign. The Prime Minister made a profusion of statements and said there was no longer any problem. He said our economy had reached its apex and we no longer had any problems as a result of the administration of the Conservative government. I do not know whether the Minister of Labour had a hand in drafting any of the election campaign messages, but his department contributed some very profound statements, statements that if they were believed-and I think they were, by a fairly large number of the electorate-would lead unquestionably to a Conservative government being re-elected. On June 16, I think it was-in any case it was the Friday prior

to the election-Conservative party headquarters issued a news release purporting to emanate from the Department of Labour in Ottawa. It said:
The Department of Labour economists flatly predict that June -will see for all those who want to work full employment in Canada.
How does that square with the facts which the minister himself brought to light this afternoon? I took the trouble to put a question down on the order paper this session. It asked:
Did the Department of Labour issue a press release in June, 1962, which indicated that there would be full employment in Canada during that month.
Of course, as I expected, the answer was, no. The same news release emanating from Ottawa had this to say:
We repeat-
They were repeating an earlier statement.
-the bureau of statistics this morning announces the greatest increase in jobs in any month in Canadian history.
In an earlier address to this house given, I believe, during the so-called budget debate, I referred to this matter as being an instance of duplicity on the part of the government. I am using it now to show that the actual facts regarding our unemployment situation are not as the government wished to have us believe either at that time or since. I showed then, on the basis of the actual figures, that the statement which had been put out was untrue, that is, that the actual figures were not correct. I also took the trouble to put down a question asking whether the dominion bureau of statistics had announced in the month of June, 1962, that the greatest increase of jobs in any month in Canada's history had taken place in the month of May. Again, the answer was a categorical no. This afternoon the Minister of Labour himself proved to us that this was a sham- that it was merely advertising which was contrary to the provisions of the Canada Elections Act and contrary to those of the Broadcasting Act.
The minister has said that the rate of unemployment today, that is, the percentage of unemployment to the labour force, is 6.3 per cent. He says that this is average or normal, because it was 6.4 per cent at the same time last year. Let us admit, then, that our economy is sick. Because its temperature has improved by one tenth of one degree, does not give us anything about which we can be satisfied. If this is the attitude of this government, that we should be satisfied with an unemployment figure of 6.4 per cent at that time of the year, in December, when we had the most open fall or early winter of the last half century, it is no wonder that our economy is failing to

move forward as it should. By the time the January figures or even the December figures are published we shall undoubtedly find that the unemployment picture is much changed and, perhaps, unemployment will amount to more than 8 per cent. Is this a situation which the government is prepared to accept as normal? If it is, it is time for the present administration to remove itself from office and make way for another which would be prepared to face the facts of our economic situation.
We have in recent days heard reports of a member of the cabinet, who is apparently not answerable to this house, making statements abroad that those of us who say our economy is not in a good condition should consider our position as Canadians. I am referring, of course to the so-called barefoot boy from Bay street who went to Toronto to lecture the Liberals on the attitude they should take toward this government. I have here a copy of the Toronto daily Star of January 29.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) has just tabled the estimates of his department, as prepared in April last, and as revised at the beginning of this session.
Normally, those estimates should have been considered and approved during the last spring session, if parliament had not been dissolved at that time. Therefore, we now have to discuss and approve expenditures of which ten twelfths have already been approved, which puts us in a rather unusual situation. In fact, I think it would be pointless to lose precious time in discussing at

length the figures which are now submitted to us, and I can assure the house that we, Social Crediters, are prepared to co-operate in order to keep the debate within a strict minimum.
We also take into consideration the fact that these estimates will be referred to the public accounts committee where they will be closely scrutinized. So I see no reason to prolong indefinitely this discussion which, for all intents and purposes, will produce nothing and will not make the government change anything to what has already been submitted.
Besides, I am sure that all hon. members would be far more interested in a discussion of the estimates that the minister will submit in his next budget, for then we would be in a better position to judge the attitude that the government will consider taking in relation to the problem of unemployment and of economic and industrial development in Canada.
Mr. Chairman, we note that the amount of money put at the disposal of the department has more than doubled; in fact, it has jumped from $53,935,000 to $112,809,000. I think that, in principle, all members will agree that such an increase was desirable. However, the only remark I should like to make is about the distribution of that money among the various items of that department.
I should like to deal in particular with the technical training assistance, which is increasingly important, and of which the provinces do not seem to have benefited in a fair way.
The figures issued recently have shown that, out of an amount of $285 million, provided by the federal government, the province of Ontario alone secured $186 million, while the province of Quebec received only $13 million. This is quite significant of the problems brought about by a centralized administration which cannot think of any legislation or regulation in terms of the needs of all provinces.
This legislation, having been developed by the federal government, without any detailed study by the provinces, has allowed a particular province to benefit substantially from the situation, to obtain much more than the others, due to the fact that this legislation was developed and drafted in terms of the needs of that particular province.
At his recent meeting with provincial representatives, the minister had the opportunity of listening to their grievances on this
Supply-Labour
particular matter, and I hope he has given full consideration to the requests which have been made to him.
In my opinion, it would have been proper to consider the possibility of maintaining and increasing that assistance of 75 per cent to the construction cost of technical schools in the provinces. This would allow the other provinces, which have not originally benefited from the advantages of this legislation, to benefit this year from that federal offer. That also brings to light the fact that the provinces alone have not enough income at this time, to carry out their tasks with regard to vocational training and the training of the teachers who are to give courses in the technical schools. Here again, we have the problem of the distribution of taxes and of the whole fiscal field.
Mr. Chairman, the training of workers is one of the many aspects of the problem created by the unemployment which now prevails in this country. We seem unable to solve this problem. To increase the number of jobs is the main objective now, so that we may eliminate unemployment.
It is all right to appoint research bodies, to send missions abroad to examine the situation and to propose training people for a higher level of efficiency by increasing the number of our technical schools. The fact remains, however, that all those measures are subject to an increase of employment opportunities in this country.
How can we increase the number of jobs in Canada? To enlarge our plants and to create new ones seems to be the only solution at this time, and I wonder how the government intends to obtain that increase in production through the increase in the number of our industries.
The government made an inquiry, sent missions in Europe and in almost every country in the world to observe what is being done there to deal with unemployment and promote industrial development.
It seems to me that all those things are closely related to a new conception that we must have as regards the needs and the goals of labour.
Here I should like to bring to the attention of the committee an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Star and which dealt precisely with a problem related to the present unemployment situation. And, in this regard, I shall refer to disarmament, about which so much is being said nowadays. A world wide campaign is going on at the present time for complete disarmament. Well, that editorial

Supply-Labour
mentions that, at this moment, armed forces and war industries are providing jobs for 50 million men and women. Therefore, although in our hearts we all want disarmament, it is normal for our administrators to ask themselves how they would provide for 50 million additional employees because, even now, our leaders cannot organize our economic system in such a way that the available labour force will be kept busy.
It makes one wonder whether our administrators are really serious when they ask for world disarmament. Do they really want that disarmament which, after all, would create other problems for them, much greater problems probably, in the field of employment?
That brings up the problem of the false economic conception we now have, of the false conception of the purpose of labour. If, at the present time, we can provide a livelihood and pay salaries to 50 million men and women in the armed forces, when, to all practical purposes, they do not offer any services nor produce any consumer goods whatever, I wonder why we cannot provide them with a livelihood outside of that war production and those armed services.
I know, Mr. Chairman, that it is a very complicated problem which calls for a thorough retraining of that mass of people who, for many years, have performed military functions.
I know that the governments which, at present, realize this problem and consider such a contingency, are wondering how to provide the jobs which would be required at that time, due to the discharge of these military people who would come on the labour market, which would likely cause as great a threat as the present nuclear threat. That is why we can see in the world today economically strong countries, for instance the western countries, a war policy being promoted because it serves their interests and it hides a colossal failure with regard to the economy and the understanding of human needs.
I am sure, Mr. Chairman, that as long as we consider work as an end in itself, we shall always encounter these same problems.
To go back to the possibility of increasing the number of jobs here in Canada by increasing the number of our industries, unfortunately I must say that now, with the present world economic doctrine, with all those circumstances which exist, with all the

international agreements, I think that the government will have to impose tariff protection measures for new industries. It will have to do it on a temporary basis, so as to enable those new industries to compete with foreign producers, within our home market.
At present, there are foreign manufacturers who sell in Canada. We should interest Canadian businessmen to manufacture those products sold in Canada by foreign manufacturers.
I know very well, of course, that it is impossible to make everything we need and everything we consume. From an economic standpoint, it is probably difficult to do so. But I think that between the present situation and an improved one, there is a long way, and we can work and achieve some objectives.
The possibility of resorting to tariff measures to help our industries undoubtedly represents one solution. I would not say it is the best solution, but it is one of them and of course, it should be temporary.
Now, there would also be special tax abatements. There would be the accelerated depreciation of investments and a wider use of the industrial development bank which I think does not play its part any too well. That bank should not be only an industrial development bank, but also an industrial creation bank, because we shall certainly need funds to finance those new industries.
At this time, I should like to quote an item which I noted recently in a newspaper. It is about an economist who was considering the economic situation of Canada in relation to our external trade. He was analysing our monetary deficit. He was pointing out the interests and dividends we pay each year on American investments in Canada. He was mentioning our imbalance of trade with the United States which amounts to $1 billion and several hundreds of million dollars each year, with respect only to interests and dividends paid on American investments in Canada.
According to him, we are not even able at the present time to correct this imbalance; we are even unable to suppress its cause.
Only yesterday, one could read in the papers that in 1962, American investments in Canada reached $1,100 million. This means that we will have to pay to our southern neighbours additional interests which, in any case, sooner or later, will always show up in the continual deficits we have known in the past and which will keep on increasing as long as we will not change our economic concept respecting

the development of our industries and of our natural resources by Canadians and, as far as possible, with Canadian capital.
I feel, however, that the industrial development bank will be the most appropriate organization, after its regulations are amended, to promote the economic development of Canada.
I know that Canadians have savings which they could invest in industry, but at the present time, the different levels of government, through their various bond issues, create a scarcity of capital available for the development of our industries.
Then, if the government cannot think of any other way of financing its management, well, it will have to be in a position to create the source of capital it needs to make the development of our industries possible.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, I am not referring to the participation of the representative of Her Majesty the Queen to the opening ceremony of parliament. I am just talking about a time-consuming and costly ceremonial.
I merely wish to point out that in the twentieth century, we should no longer have to observe the sort of formalities in honour at the court of Louis the Fourteenth. To revert to the principle of my motion, I suggest that the throne speech debate should not take place. In my opinion, this eight day period used by the leaders of opposition parties to derive probably some degree of political capital, but which promotes in no way the public welfare, should be abolished, thus enabling us to consider without delay the business of the house and to hasten passage of legislation brought before the house.
I had the opportunity to attend the opening session of the United Nations and I found out that in this world assembly, no time is lost on such a trivial matter as the reply to the president's speech.
I also suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the time allowed to hon. members be cut down from 30 to 15 minutes. Moreover, the sittings should be from 2 to 7 p.m. instead of from 2.30 to 6 p.m. and from 8 to 10 p.m. Thus the members could attend to their work as representatives of the people, in the evening and in the morning.
At this time of day, members introduce notices of motions and everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, that all of them get a first class burial.
I think that all hon. members are of the opinion that this time is put at our disposal merely to give us the opportunity to make speeches, and the administration of the public business does not benefit from it in any way. The time provided for the consideration of private members' business could be abolished, which would give us an extra hour a day.

Special Committee on Procedure
If some do not agree that this hour should be abolished, we might get in touch with the other parties and find out if one of them intends to kill a motion. Under the circumstances, the sponsors of such motions could withdraw them so as not to waste their time or take up the time of other hon. members.
I would also suggest, sir, that we abolish debates on resolutions submitted to the house by committees. We do not have the bills before us during such debates and that is a loss of time because such legislation comes before the house at a later date and we then have to engage in another time-consuming debate.
Consideration should also be given to shortening the question period.
The question period, that lasts over an hour and a half at times, has become a real free for all. In my opinion, it could be limited to half an hour; each party would have the right to ask only so many questions and each member would be allowed only one question. We could thus dispatch more expeditiously the public business. We would not see ridiculous situations happen every day, which has been the case since the beginning of this session.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this motion

I can say at the outset that I am in favour of it. I think the time has arrived when the special committee should be reconvened in order to consider further the rules under which we carry on business.
It was mentioned in the speech from the throne that the committee would be reconvened, but in view of the initial remarks of the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapdelaine) in which he bypassed this formality, I presume he did not wish to refer to it. Nevertheless that particular proposition is in the speech from the throne, in somewhat similar terms. In any case I am in agreement with both propositions.
I think the reason for inefficiency in this house is that we spend many hours discusss-ing matters on which there is agreement, just for some procedural advantage. This is the sum and substance of all our difficulties, and we can avoid a lot of the lost time if we are able to remove some of the advantages that accrue from talking on things on which there is general agreement.
I should like to mention a few now in the hope that this committee, if set up, will consider them. The first subject with which I wish to deal is the private members' hour, which we are in at this moment. I have always felt that a good deal of time is wasted in private members' hour by hon. members carrying on a debate for the purpose of filling in the one hour allotted. In this particular matter I accept equal responsibility with a number of my colleagues.

I am glad that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) gives me first place somewhere. However, Mr. Speaker, this is one of our major problems. 1 think it could be cured and I am going to put forward a proposal in connection with private members' hour which I think will help. When the rules were last revised private members' hour was put on daily. That was a great advantage because now a tremendous number of notices of motion are put before the house. Before this amendment only about four private members' notices of motion ever came before the house, and those generally were talked on for a whole day. The present system is certainly much better. However, I would suggest that we could improve it if, after all hon. members who indicate that they wish to speak on the subject have spoken, and no

other person appears ready to rise and continue the debate, the minister under whose jurisdiction the particular subject comes, or his parliamentary secretary, were to rise and take one of three choices. First, he could indicate that the government accepts the resolution or bill in general terms. Second, he could indicate that the government rejects the resolution or bill. In the case of either of these two alternatives the question should immediately be put, subject to the right of the sponsor to close the debate. The third choice I would suggest is that the minister could state that the government desires to give further study to the resolution or bill. In such event the minister or parliamentary secretary could move the adjournment of the debate.
This would not in any way be limiting the rights of private members on private members' hour, because this situation would only arise if no other hon. member appeared ready or willing to speak on the subject, in which event the minister or his parliamentary secretary could rise in the same manner as does an hon. member who closes the debate and state that the matter is worthy of consideration and will receive further study; and the debate should be adjourned for the time being. I think this would be very helpful because the house could then go on to another resolution or bill. In some of these cases only one or two hon. members are prepared and willing to speak on the subject, and sometimes these matters are brought forward in a hurry due to the previous motion or motions having been stood over. I think in this way we could save a good deal of time. As I have said, I am the first to admit that on various occasions I have been guilty of speaking on private members' hour when perhaps I was in favour of the resolution or bill and might better have let it come to a vote. But we have to be honest about this. Because of the way the procedure is set up it is sometimes advantageous that certain resolutions should not come to a vote. With this very honest approach to the matter I believe we could go a long way toward making private members' hour more efficient and effective.
I have another suggestion for saving time, Mr. Speaker. I think that the question of appeals from decisions of the Speaker should be reconsidered. I believe that the Speaker's decision should be final and not subject to appeal to the house.

I will come to the point in just one moment. The main reason is that appeals to the house never decide whether the Speaker was right or wrong. They are never voted upon on the basis of whether the Speaker made a correct decision. I have observed over a period of almost six years the question of appeals from decisions of Speakers and have noticed that in every case the appeal is voted upon on party lines. This does not mean anything. It does not mean that the Speaker was either right or wrong in his decision. I feel that in order to have an orderly growth of a body of precedent in the House of Commons the Speaker should make a decision to the best of his ability and that decision should be final. I say again that when voting on an appeal the minds of hon. members in the house, I am sure, are not always on the correctness of the Speaker's decision or on precedent, but are on other matters which possibly are quite beyond the correctness of the decision. I think there is a great deal of inconsistency in connection with appeals to the house from the Speaker's decisions. We find in one parliament that a certain ruling by the Speaker, which may have been in accordance with precedent, is reversed in another parliament simply because of the system of voting on party lines. In this way different conclusions are reached in different parliaments.
Therefore it does not follow that any body of precedent can be established or that an appeal from the Speaker's ruling means anything at all as far as the correctness of the decision itself is concerned. I think that errors which Speakers make and have made in the past are matters all of us must accept in electing a Speaker to make decisions on our behalf. I do feel that the Speaker's decisions should not be subject to appeal to the house.
In a similar category is the question of appeals from decisions of committee chairmen. As I understand the situation, Mr. Speaker, we are in a considerable state of confusion in this house with regard to an appeal from a decision of a chairman of a standing committee. There is nothing in our rules of practice and procedure relating to appeals from committee chairmen and there has never been, to my knowledge, an established practice with regard to whether there is an appeal, and if so, to whom. In the first section of our rules it is stated that if nothing is provided to the contrary in our rules, the practice of the House of Commons at Westminster shall be followed. My point in drawing attention to these things is that these are reasons why a committee should be set up. I am setting forth what I believe to be inequities in our present procedure, deficiencies which could be corrected by such a committee. I believe these are perfectly good reasons for supporting the motion.
Perhaps I might continue on the subject I had raised earlier with reference to appeals from decisions by committee chairmen. The present situation is confusing. Under its rules, the house of commons in the United Kingdom has no provisions for such appeals. If we refer to the United Kingdom rules-and there is nothing in our own rules to deal with this particular case-we find there is no provision for an appeal from rulings of the Chair, and it follows there is no appeal from the ruling of a committee chairman in Canada. I have taken this position in the committee of which I have the honour to be chairman. Even if there were the right of 
appeal there is some doubt whether the appeal should be to the house or to the committee itself. I do not wish to pursue this matter but I think it is a subject which might well be considered by a committee such as is proposed.
There is one other thing we might well do to prevent too much jockeying for position during the session and to facilitate the expeditious dispatch of business. I believe the time has come when the proposed date of the prorogation of the session of parliament should be announced at or near the beginning of each session and that unless the session is extended by a vote of two thirds of the members it should be prorogued on that date. The responsibility for delay, extension, failure to bring forward legislation, failure to act on legislation and so on could not then be shifted back and forth between one party and another. It would then be up to the house to conclude its business within the time allotted. I think that if such an announcement were made it would prove of great advantage.
I also think the time has come when the length of the sessions of this house should be considered. Certainly, as a collateral question, the subject of members' pay has come up as was mentioned by the proposer of this motion. But I think that if the work of the session were dealt with expeditiously and if members could return to their private business for at least half their time during the year, they would have no financial difficulties. I certainly believe that if such a procedure were adopted it would prove satisfactory. Should certain matters arise requiring an extension of time, this could be arranged by a two-thirds vote.
In the same vein I would suggest that no legislation should be introduced later than two weeks prior to the proposed date of prorogation. I think if this suggestion were adopted the house would be in a position to conclude its business in good order and, when the time arrives, there would be no last minute legislation likely to warrant extending the time of sitting of the house except, as I have said, in the case of an emergency, in which situation a vote of two thirds of the members would be required.
These are just a few of the many subjects which require discussion in such a committee as is proposed. I support the motion. I hope the committee will be set up and that these matters will be dealt with. I think this is more than a routine debate and a routine resolution. It is a most serious matter. Right now, as far as this house is concerned, we are wasting time. But who is to blame? It is easy to throw accusations back and forth that it is this party or that party which is causing

the difficulty. We have to face the situation which confronts us. I think the time has come when it must be faced and the only way in which it can be done, as far as I know, is by revising the rules so as to impose on ourselves some restriction to prevent our wasting the time of this house and the people's money.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext:
The theme of the motion by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapdelaine) is that the House of Commons ought to make haste speedily, that it ought to engage in a more expeditious dispatch of public business. He suggests that the way to do this is to set up a committee on procedure to consult with Your Honour and to effect changes in the rules.
We all want to save time. We all want to shorten debate and shorten sessions, provided this objective is reached without failing to achieve an even more important objective, namely the preservation of the rights of private members of the House of Commons. One of the main purposes of the rules is to protect the rights of individual members elected in their individual capacity to serve their constituents. The rules also provide a systematic method of dealing with public business and they ensure that there is an opportunity as the life of each session unfolds for each item of public business to be discussed in a systematic way. The rules under which we operate have been tried and tested by experience and I believe it is a mistake on the part of hon. members, and especially on the part of the mover of this motion, to believe that all our parliamentary difficulties and frustrations flow from faulty rules and that these difficulties could be removed by a formal change in the rules.
I was surprised that the hon. member should recommend that the opening ceremony in connection with parliament ought to be abolished, that we ought to save a few hours and thereby deprive ourselves of a reminder for example, of the symbolic importance of the mace and of the importance of the first bill the Prime Minister introduces. These are ceremonies, but they remind us in a short space of time of the struggle that has taken place over the centuries to reach a position where we have a free parliament, where free discussion is possible. On reflection, I am not surprised, because this attitude is consistent with the anti-parliamentary, anti-discussion approach which has been manifested by the hon. member's particular group since they came into the House of Commons.

The hon. member is not the first member of parliament who has tried his hand at streamlining our work. He is not the first among the present members of this house who has made sincere proposals to streamline the work of the House of Commons. The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) not so many years ago held out great hope that the expansion of the committees system would make parliament a more effective instrument in dealing with the public business. If I may quote from a comment made by the right hon. gentleman in 1960, he stated as follows:
In pursuance of our desire to bring about an expansion in the opportunities for all members of the house as a whole to make their contribution, we have in the last two sessions set up a number of committees ... I hope we will be able to expand the system in this regard to the end that we can use committees to a larger extent than in the past, thus rendering parliament more effective.
The house has attempted in the organization of its work in the past five years to make the committees system a more effective instrument and to relieve the House of Commons of certain burdens. I noticed that the Prime Minister confessed with candour not so many days ago in this house that the hopes he had held for an expansion of the committees system were not realized, and that this effort he had in mind had not reached its objective. I believe there is a resistance among members of parliament in transferring from this national forum to other subsidiary bodies certain functions, including committees of the house, and I believe there will be a resistance to the changing of any rules that hon. members might feel will in the future restrict at a critical time the right of any individual member to express his opinions.
In saying that, Mr. Speaker, I am aware that the committee on procedure sitting under your predecessors has accomplished a good deal in streamlining, and especially reducing, the time spent on debate. That work was done, as we know, with the active co-operation of Liberal members sitting on that committee. Private members' days have been reduced in number. The length of speeches has been reduced. The number of days spent on the budget debate and on the address in reply has been reduced. As all this has happened, serious parliamentary observers have wondered how far the erosion of the rights of private members is going to continue.

Special Committee on Procedure Where is it going to stop? We have had from the hon. member today a proposal that we abolish altogether the address in reply, which is the first opportunity, maybe the only opportunity, new members elected to the House of Commons will have to address the Commons on behalf of their respective constituencies. Abolish that altogether, is the view of the Social Credit party. Again they say, abolish the private members hour, which time has already narrowed down, but is still there to give private members an opportunity of bringing before the house subjects in which they are interested. Even though no action might be taken on them, at least public opinion is formed and views are expressed.

Well, I think, Mr. Speaker, I have answered that question by anticipation. I ask myself whether there are important changes which can be made in the rules of the house which would effect real economies in time. We have reduced the time on the address. Shall we reduce it two more days and thereby deny more members the opportunity to take part? Shall we reduce the budget debate and thereby deny more members an opportunity to take part? Shall we reduce the number of supply motions and deny private members an opportunity to raise votes of non-confidence against the government? Shall we reduce the number of readings of a bill? Shall we have only one reading and pass the bill at one stage? This is the kind of important change which will have to be made in the rules in order to effect real economies.
Mr. Speaker, in the light of the remarks made by the hon. gentleman, and in the light of his desire to achieve economies through cutting down opportunities for debate, I was surprised how fully and effectively the members of his party have taken advantage of their opportunities for addressing the House of Commons since they have come here, and how fully they have been reported in the press of the country.

I do not believe that the work of this session has been so unimpressive that it ought to lead to an immediate drastic change in the rules. I think one of the important matters we must remember is that the government of the day has a place in the organization of the business of the house. It is the government, and nobody else, which decides every day the business that will be dealt with the next day. All the opposition can do is to react: it cannot initiate. It is not the responsibility of the opposition to organize the business. It is because the business of the house has been so badly organized that we have had only five days on the main estimates, and only one supply motion. There is frustration among members of the house. I appreciate the point you made, Your Honour; but surely in a discussion of the way in which to deal expeditiously with public business we must ask ourselves the question whether this purpose can best be served through a change in the rules or whether there is another way which might yield greater results. I think that establishes the relevancy of my comments to the effect that the government is responsible for the agenda. If the house does not get the agenda, it cannot move ahead. I could give many illustrations but, in the light of your admonition, Mr. Speaker, I will give only one more.
In the session of 1960-61, the opposition agreed to waive the debate in reply. The opposition gave up its rights and it was unanimously agreed upon by all members of the house. How many bills were passed in the first 60 days? Six bills were passed. What was the reason for that situation? The reason was that the government was not ready. The government could not bring on its legislation and the house wasted its time in fruitless discussion, with no results. That is why I say that, although we will agree to the setting up of a committee on procedure and will co-operate with other members in making
Special Committee on Procedure whatever changes are to be made, nevertheless there are other more important ways by which the public business can be expeditiously dispatched.
I agree that certain constructive ideas are coming forward in this debate. A suggestion has been made by the mover that we ought to reduce the time of the question period. I go along with that idea. I am sure Your Honour would appreciate a suggestion in the committee on procedure that some arrangement, possibly on an experimental basis, could reduce the oral question period to half an hour per day.
