Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member who last spoke, namely the hon. member for Invemess-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen), was a little bit less than fair to the mover of the resolution. I think the mover intended to improve parliamentary procedures and to make this parliament more effective. I do not think he proposed in any sense to cut down discussion or to abridge the rights of private members or of parliament.
I support this resolution because I, as I think do many other hon. members, feel strongly that this parliament, being the central institution of democracy, should function with just as much efficiency as is possible. If the procedures in this parliament are obsolete and lend themselves to endless repetition and to long winded and unproductive discussion, then to that extent parliament itself falls into disrepute. In suggesting, in accordance with what has already been promised in the speech from the throne, the setting up of this committee, I feel that the hon. member intended, as do we in this group, to improve the procedures of parliament. We believe it is urgent to improve the procedures of this parliament and not in any way to abridge its rights. It struck me that the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond showed some of the complacency and conservatism which one also associates with his party.
I suggest that the committee should be set up. I wish to make one suggestion, namely that many of its members be new members of this house. In discussion with members in all parts of the house who have been here for some time I have observed that they have relapsed into a state of despondency, despair and discouragement, and have become inured to the procedures of the house. They have got themselves into a condition

Special Committee on Procedure in which they do not believe anything can be done, and sometimes they doubt whether it should be done. As one of the new members I wish to say, and I believe I share this view with many new members, that I am a little bit horrified by the time that is wasted, and by the amount of repetitiveness in debate, which I believe brings this house into disrepute. I suggest one reform that is obvious, namely that we should not give way to our national Canadian weakness for long windedness in speeches.
As hon. members will recall, apart from the formalities, we started this session with a three hour address from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), followed by a three hour address from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). I am saying nothing disrespectful to these two gentlemen when I suggest that their speeches would have been infinitely more effective if they had taken not more than an hour each. It is my conviction that all the members of this house would make more effective speeches if, instead of speaking for their full time of 40 minutes, they disciplined themselves and spoke for half that time. I understand that in the mother of parliaments there is no rule as to the length of speeches, but that it is the custom of members who speak to speak for only 15 or 20 minutes. Should they exceed that time, not only are they drowned out by their colleagues but the Speaker seldom, if ever, recognizes them again.
I know that is not a responsibility we can put upon you, Mr. Speaker, because, by long custom of this house, it has been the practice for each hon. member who speaks, whether he has anything to say or not, to speak at interminable length and to the full extent permitted by the rules. I suggest that one real reform would be to cut in half the time allowed for speeches. By that means we would get more speeches from more members and better speeches, than we get at the present time. There would be an improvement in our democratic procedure which might save time. I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that saving time is the only object of reforming the rules. We could save time, of course; but I am suggesting that streamlining the procedure would not only save time but make the time we do spend more productive and more worth while.
I have often noticed that those who have to speak in 20 minutes speak a lot better than those who are given 40 minutes. I have not addressed this house very often myself, but on one occasion I realized it was seven minutes to six o'clock, the time it is now, and I had a 20 minute speech prepared. I boiled it down to seven minutes, and several members of the

house were kind enough to tell me it was by far the best speech that I had made in the house.

Mr. Speaker, I am going to practise my own principles, but by trying to confine myself to about 10 minutes rather than seven minutes. The recommendations I have made should be considered by this committee.
The question of committees has been brought up. I do not care whether or not it has been tried before. I suggest most seriously that the committees system should be employed more effectively than it has been. I remember thinking it was a great honour to be appointed to the committee on external affairs, and that as a new member I might learn something. In four months, Mr. Speaker, that committee has never met. What sort of system do we have? We have members who are anxious to find out about these subjects that concern all members who have been appointed to various committees, presumably because they have some special interest in the subject; but they have no opportunity to learn about them through the effective working of committees. If the system has been tried and found wanting, then let it be tried again, because in my respectful submission it would vastly improve the efficiency of the members of the house.
I am not singing a new song, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Cardin, a Liberal cabinet minister, said in 1943 that the rules were obsolete and that there was an urgent necessity for changes in procedure. Just to show that I pick authorities impartially, Mr. John Bracken described procedure in the Canadian parliament as being still in the oxcart stage of half a century ago. I know there have been some changes made but in my submission they have not been enough and have not gone far enough.

Somebody says "the voice of experience". Some of us have had experience outside of this house as well as in it, and I suggest that outside this house the procedures of the house would be regarded as intolerable, wasteful of the time of members and urgently needing reform. I have in front of me a book by Professor Dawson entitled "Procedure in the Canadian House of Commons". Having referred to all the revisions that have been made hitherto he goes on to say:
These revisions, however welcome, are only partial ones and leave many of the important defects of procedure untouched. The house still takes too long to do a relatively small^ amount of work. Debate during most of each session remains largely disorganized and repetitive. The committee system could be used to greater effect. The house

does not give proper scrutiny to the public accounts and the estimates. These important problems are with the house today and seem likely to remain so indefinitely into the future.
That is the view of an impartial observer outside the house and my experience in the house, brief as it is, makes me believe it entirely justified. To those members, and I am sure this includes all members, who believe in the essential importance of parliament as an instrument for the welfare of the Canadian people I suggest that reform is urgently necessary, if this institution is not to fall into disrepute. There is still time to vote on this resolution, Mr. Speaker. I have now spoken for only 10 minutes so I will obey my own injunction and sit down.

Mr. Speaker, I deplore the fact that the hon. member who just resumed his seat, while advocating freedom of speech, prevented a member from another group to express his views on this proposal.
In my opinion the purpose of the mover of this motion is most commendable and I believe that it fills an urgent need to reduce useless loss of time and to enable us to do constructive work.
Mr. Speaker, I am most surprised at the stand taken by our friends in the Liberal party, and more particularly to hear the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Mac-Eachen) say that the motion should not restrict the liberty of members to express their views before the house on all the amendments to be made to the standing orders.
I also deplore the use the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond made of the word freedom, because we, Conservatives, are not responsible for applying the closure rule. We remember the now famous pipe line debate. I cannot see how the Liberals, who do not like to be reminded of the circumstances which surrounded that debate, can now support the advisability of amending the procedure of the house.
I do not feel either that we should restrict freedom of speech, but after the remarks of the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond about freedom and the intention of the house

Business of the House to reduce the members freedom of speech, I must take exception to some of his statements.
I appreciate that some members of the Liberal opposition would profit enormously by keeping their seats during the debates of this house, particularly so when 95 per cent of them have nothing to say about the business submitted to us.

I should have reminded the house before this of what I said a moment ago about partisan considerations.
It now being six o'clock, the hour appointed for consideration of private members' business is expired and the house shall revert to the business interrupted at five o'clock.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext: If I may be permitted, respectfully, Mr. Speaker, to raise a question of privilege for just one moment, I suggest that the idea that any debate in this house should be non-partisan is foreign to our whole parliamentary system.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON PROCEDURE
speechtext: I fail to see that the question of privilege is a question of privilege. The hon. member is putting forward a point of view.

Mr. Speaker, I would think it would be a convenience to have in Hansard again the business for tomorrow and Friday. I have read what the hon. gentleman said last night and I would ask him if he could be quite specific-he seemed to be last night but I was not quite certain after reading his words -that there will be a supply motion on Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow and Friday we will continue discussion of the estimates, the Department of Labour and the Post Office Department. If those are finished I will call a third. On Monday and Tuesday we will have a supply motion. I should say that starting on Monday we will have a supply motion because it does not have to run for the two full days, although that is quite normal.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, January 31, 1963
